title: Milestone: Knowledge, Mind and Morals
objective: After this level you can connect the first half's traditions, theories of knowledge, views of the mind and moral theories into one map of philosophy's big questions.
summary: Ethics offers three main answers (consequences, duty, character), plus care; metaethics asks whether morality is relative, depends on God, or can follow from facts.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to fold the map.
cards.body: You’ve met theories of what is real, how we know and what a self is. This milestone lays out the moral half, the part that asks how to live, as one map.

cards.headline: Three answers to one good deed
cards.body: Someone in need should obviously be helped. But why? A utilitarian points to consequences: helping maximizes well-being. A deontologist points to duty, a moral rule. A virtue ethicist points to character: helping is charitable or kind. These are the three major approaches in normative ethics. Care ethics, set against the rule and consequence approaches, starts from relationships instead.

items.label: Consequences
points: Bentham: pain and pleasure are our masters
Mill: some pleasures are higher in kind

items.label: Duty
points: Kant: could everyone act on your maxim?
Kant: never treat people merely as means

items.label: Character
points: Aristotle: courage is a mean between two vices
Aristotle: virtue is built by practice

cards.headline: The floor underneath
cards.body: Below all of these sits metaethics. It steps back from particular moral debates to ask what morality itself is. Are there moral facts? Are moral standards culturally relative? Does morality depend on God’s commands? Can an ought follow from an is? Here Level 2’s metaphysics, the study of what exists, and epistemology, the study of knowledge, turn to ethics.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway there
learned: How Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers first asked what is real, what a self is and how to live.
Why Descartes’s doubt stopped at “I am, I exist”, and why Gettier’s lucky cases broke a classic definition.
What Mary’s room asks about the mind, and how the ability hypothesis answers it.
How consequences, duty and character give different reasons to help, and why morality’s roots are debated.

questions.prompt: Where did India’s Carvaka materialists say consciousness comes from?

options.label: From Brahman, the reality under everything
From an eternal soul
options.rationale: The Carvakas denied any such soul.

options.label: From the material body
From the gods’ commands
options.rationale: The Carvakas trusted perception, not the gods.

questions.explanation: The Carvakas argued that consciousness is a product of the material body: no body, no mind.

questions.prompt: Descartes let his imagined deceiver fool him even about two and three making five. Why couldn’t the deceiver make him wrong that he exists?

options.label: Being deceived needs someone there to be deceived
His senses showed him that he had a body
options.rationale: The senses were already in doubt after the dream argument.

options.label: The people around him agreed that he existed
options.rationale: Other people were as open to doubt as anything else.

options.label: The deceiver was only a figure in a dream he was having
options.rationale: The deceiver was meant to reach further than dreams.

questions.explanation: If the deceiver is deceiving me, then I exist: “I am, I exist” is true whenever I put it forward or conceive it.

questions.prompt: Smith’s belief about the man with ten coins was true, believed and carefully justified. Why did Gettier’s case still count against defining knowledge that way?

options.label: Smith’s evidence was too weak to count as justified
options.rationale: He had good evidence and reasoned carefully.

options.label: The belief turned out to be false
options.rationale: It was true: Smith had ten coins too.

options.label: Smith never really believed it
options.rationale: He did believe it; all three legs stood.

options.label: What made it true was luck Smith knew nothing about

questions.explanation: All three conditions held, yet the belief was true by luck, so most epistemologists agreed justified true belief isn’t enough for knowledge.

questions.prompt: Mary knows every physical fact about color vision but has never seen red. If she learns something when she first sees it, what did Jackson conclude in 1982?

options.label: Her science of vision was out of date
options.rationale: She had all the physical information there is.

options.label: Not all information is physical, so physicalism is false
She gains a skill, such as recognizing red, not a fact
options.rationale: That’s the ability hypothesis, a reply to Jackson.

options.label: Color vision can never be studied by science
options.rationale: Mary studied it completely; the question is what that leaves out.

questions.explanation: Jackson argued that if all-knowing Mary still learns what seeing red is like, her physical knowledge was incomplete, so physicalism is false. Lewis and Nemirow reply that she gains abilities, not facts.

questions.prompt: A friend helps a stranger in need because doing so is kind and charitable. The approach that explains the act that way is _____.

options.label: consequentialism
options.rationale: That would point to the best consequences.

options.label: deontology
options.rationale: That would point to a moral rule.

options.label: virtue ethics
relativism
options.rationale: That’s a view about moral truth, not a reason to help.

questions.explanation: Pointing to the kindness or charity of the act is the virtue ethicist’s answer, focused on character.

questions.prompt: Match each approach with what it points to when explaining why we should help someone in need.
questions.explanation: A utilitarian points to consequences, a deontologist to duty, a virtue ethicist to character, and care ethics starts from relationships.

questions.prompt: Glaucon’s story of the ring of Gyges led to a challenge. What did Glaucon finally ask Socrates to show?

options.label: That justice always brings the best reputation and rewards
That the ring really existed
options.rationale: The ring was a story, not a claim.

options.label: That injustice is better if unseen
options.rationale: That’s the view Glaucon wanted refuted.

options.label: That justice is worth having in itself, seen or unseen

questions.explanation: Glaucon, backed by his brother Adeimantus, asked Socrates to show what justice does to its possessor in itself, whether seen or unseen by gods and men.
